source.title: Narrow Misalignment is Hard, Emergent Misalignment is Easy

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether fine-tuning on narrow harmful medical advice generalizes to unrelated questions, using a different narrow task from the insecure-code original and adding KL-regularized adapter experiments.
record.gate_note: The post refers to a table of misalignment percentages and plots from Training Lens, but their contents are not present in the supplied text; no values are inferred from them. The 1/4 result is explicitly attributed to Wang et al. and is not recorded as this study's result.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes a chat model on narrow bad medical advice and measures misaligned answers to unrelated general questions (about 40%). That is a V2 test with a different narrow dataset. Its main contribution, the KL-regularized narrow solutions and their loss and stability, concerns a related construct and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude the general misalignment solution is more stable and efficient than the narrow one. They offer this as a mechanistic explanation for why EM arises, and note the narrow solution reverts to EM without KL. They leave open why pretraining yields such an efficient misalignment representation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful medical advice rather than insecure code, and studies KL-regularized steering vectors and rank 1/rank 32 LoRA adapters as well as general solutions.
record.method_sensitivity: The result depends on KL regularization and data mixture: the KL-protected setup reports 0% general misalignment, while the mixed-data experiment reports emergent misalignment at a 1/6 harmful share and ineffective learning below that. The small-data adapter experiments also report limitations, including lower bad-medical-advice rates and occasional Mandarin-only misaligned outputs.

fits_no_version.finding: KL regularization against the chat model on parallel non-medical data yields up to 65% bad medical advice with 0% general misalignment. With 1:12 dilution, general misalignment is 0% and bad advice is under 5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM can be prevented by KL-regularizing behaviour in other domains during narrow harmful fine-tuning while still learning the narrow task.

fits_no_version.finding: General solutions reach lower training loss at lower norm and degrade less under orthogonal noise than narrow solutions, for steering vectors and rank 1 and rank 32 LoRAs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The general misalignment solution is more efficient and stable than the narrow one, explaining why fine-tuning prefers it.

fits_no_version.finding: Continuing training from narrow solutions without KL reverts to the general misaligned solution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow-only solutions are unstable under further unregularized training and drift to EM.

fits_no_version.finding: Top 3 PCs of steering-vector trajectories (79% variance) cannot reproduce the misaligned behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training trajectories are not cleanly decomposable into narrow and general directions.

record.problems: The supplied post does not include the referenced table and plots, so configuration-specific percentages and numeric loss values cannot be checked. Behavioral rates are reported without uncertainty estimates. The model name and parameter count are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: The referenced general-versus-narrow misalignment percentage table and Training Lens plots are not included in the supplied text, so their configuration-level results could not be recorded. The cited 1/4 harmful-data result is attributed to Wang et al., not this study.

untested.parts: No insecure-code data or its secure/educational controls.
Only bad medical advice. Financial advice, reward hacks and number sequences are not tested.
No test of a shared direction across different fine-tunes. The PCA finding concerns a single dataset.
No inoculation framing or benign retraining. KL regularization is a different intervention.
No model-size or seed variation of the EM rate, and no coherence filtering. Footnote 4 on suppressed EM under weak KL is not quantified.

missing.what: Table of general and narrow misalignment percentages for steering vector, rank 1 and rank 32 LoRA general and narrow solutions (absent from the supplied text)
missing.locator: Training a Narrowly Misaligned Model, table

missing.what: With a lower KL coefficient, fine-tunes show 0% misalignment but EM appears when parameters are scaled up (suppressed, not absent)
Author comment: EM is most effective with single-layer adapters in central layers (20-28 of 48). Layers 29-31 give narrow, poor solutions; higher layers fail.

record.verdict_notes: LessWrong research update with no model name; the setup is a 48-layer chat model with adapters on layer 24. The 1/4 result is from Wang et al. and is excluded. The bad-medical dataset differs from Turner et al.; misalignment is averaged over held-in and held-out topics. The KL rows were moved off V2, so the reader's KL-based limits_scope label was dropped.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses harmful medical advice, not insecure code, and does not test secure-code or class-requested insecure-code controls.
Tests harmful medical advice, not bad financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
The study does not test whether one linear direction or persona feature mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
KL regularization to preserve non-medical behavior is tested, but not requested-bad-behavior framing or brief benign retraining.

The study does not test effect size across open-model sizes, coherence filters, or training stages. Its weight-perturbation loss experiment does not measure robustness of the claimed broad misaligned-answer rate.
